title: iPhone Driver's License Feature in Apple Wallet Just Launched in 16th U.S. State
content:
Starting today, Oklahoma residents can add a digital version of their driver's license to the Apple Wallet app on the iPhone and Apple Watch. The digital ID can be used to display proof of identity or age at TSA checkpoints in select airports, at select businesses, and in select apps, but the number of places where it is accepted is still quite limited.


Oklahoma is the 16th state to implement support for Apple Wallet IDs in the U.S., joining Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Georgia, Hawaii, Illinois, Iowa, Maryland, Montana, New Mexico, North Dakota, Ohio, Virginia, and West Virginia. The feature is also available in Puerto Rico and works with Japan's My Number Card.

Apple has also been preparing for the feature to go live in North Carolina and Utah in the coming months, and years ago it announced that Connecticut, Kentucky, and Mississippi were committed to launching the feature at some point.

To set up the feature, open the Wallet app on the iPhone and tap on the plus sign in the top-right corner. Next, tap on Driver's License and ID Cards, select Oklahoma from the list, and follow the on-screen steps to complete the process. Then, you can present your digital ID where it is accepted without handing over your device.


You can present an Apple Wallet ID where accepted by simply tapping your iPhone or Apple Watch on an identity reader. Then, you will be able to view the specific information being requested by the TSA or business. Only after authorizing with Face ID or Touch ID is the requested identity information released from your device.

As mentioned, you do not need to unlock, show, or hand over your device to present an Apple Wallet ID in person, ensuring user privacy.

Apple Wallet IDs are generally not accepted by law enforcement, so carrying a physical ID is still legally required for traffic stops. In addition, the number of businesses that accept Apple Wallet IDs is still quite small. At least for now, Apple Wallet IDs are designed to be a convenient alternative where they are accepted.

title: An iPhone Ultra stylus would be a colossal mistake
content:
Macworld





Apple founder Steve Jobs wasn’t a big fan of the stylus. “Who wants a stylus?” he asked at the original iPhone launch in 2007. “You have to get ’em and put ’em away, you lose ’em, yuck.” Nobody wants a stylus.” Instead, the iPhone’s interface was built around what he referred to as the best pointing device in the world: the human finger. This was a risk at the time, but the iPhone ended up doing reasonably well.
That’s not to say that Jobs’ view on the matter was definitive. Look up a YouTube clip of the stylus monologue–as I just did, to get the wording right–and you’re sure to see plenty of commenters gleefully pointing out Apple’s later change of direction. In 2015, a different CEO named Tim announced the launch of the Apple Pencil, a stylus. What an embarrassing U-turn, those commenters would have you believe. Although it’s worth bearing in mind that the Apple Pencil was designed for the iPad, not the iPhone, and to this day the company has resisted the urge to make a smartphone that can be controlled using a stylus.
That may yet change. In the latest edition of his Power On newsletter, the Bloomberg leaker Mark Gurman insists “with zero doubt” that Apple has prototyped and internally tested a special version of the Apple Pencil for its upcoming foldable iPhone. This stylus may or may not materialize when the phone is unveiled next week; at this point, Gurman considers it unlikely. But Apple evidently gave it serious consideration.
It’s nice to have the whiff of a last-minute surprise going into the September 9 event. But on balance, I hope this ends up being one of the thousand noes rather than the one yes. I think launching the iPhone Ultra as a stylus-based (or even a stylus-optional) device would be a colossal mistake. Here are six reasons why.
1. Phone styluses are annoying
It’s been 19 years since he made them, but Steve Jobs’ objections to the stylus remain valid. They’re annoying, fiddly objects, inconvenient to get out, and easy to lose. It’s an extra thing to worry about when the revolutionary joy of the 2007 iPhone was the way it unified all your tech into a single point of use. You no longer needed to carry a digital camera, an iPod, and a cellphone. Gratuitous accessories like the stylus are a regression to the bad old days.
On a larger, more work-focused device like the iPad Pro, such annoyances can be viewed as an acceptable compromise. iPads often live in a bag, and bags have side pockets for things like the Apple Pencil. If you set up your iPad for a longer work session, it’s less of a hassle, but iPhones are instant-use devices, and they don’t need random gizmos adding friction to the process.
2. Where do you store it, and how do you charge it?
One of the biggest problems with the original Apple Pencil, and one of the biggest improvements made by the 2nd-gen model in 2018, relates to storage and charging. Later versions attach magnetically to the side of an iPad and charge wirelessly, which means a) it’s always there, and b) it’s always charged when you need it. Before then, Apple Pencils were generally found at the bottom of a bag, if you could find them at all, and it was a 50/50 bet whether they would have any power. (Charging via Lightning was a design nightmare, too, but that’s another story.)
Gurman says the prototype Pencil uses a magnetic connection, but acknowledges that this isn’t ideal. “Storing the Pencil would get awkward if you want to fold the phone open and not use the accessory,” he says. I also suspect that a magnetically attached stylus will detach from the phone when in a pocket, or while being taken out of a pocket, likely resulting in one or both ending up on the floor. It doesn’t feel like a satisfactory solution, but if you don’t use magnets, you’re left with the inconvenience of the 1st-gen Pencil, or the dust-gathering inelegance of a stylus that slots into a hole. Yuck.

				
					

				
			Magnetically attaching the Apple Pencil makes sense for a tablet, but wouldn’t suit a phone.
Apple




3. Phones don’t benefit from styluses as much as tablets
The creative-targeted 2015 iPad Pro clearly benefited from the potential of a stylus, since the human finger, as even the proudest of parents will surely concede, will never rival a pen tip for artistic accuracy. But phones, and particularly iPhones, are rarely used for art, partly because their screens are smaller, and partly through habit: There’s no Apple Pencil support for the iPhone, so both users and app developers have adapted to an environment in which fingers do the work.
Are iPhone Ultra owners going to gain delightful utility from the Apple Pencil mini? I doubt it. The software isn’t there to take advantage of it, and smartphones in general don’t suit stylus input.
4. A stylus would add technical challenges Apple really doesn’t need
Considering how much money Apple is likely to ask for it (at least $2,000, and perhaps as much as $2,499), the iPhone Ultra needs to be perfect. Any hint of an Antennagate or Bendgate scenario would kill interest in an ultra-premium device, and bring a premature end to what should be a long line of foldable iPhones.
The folding screen already creates plenty of opportunity for things to go wrong (two words: crease and hinge). But as Gurman points out, making that screen stylus-sensitive ramps the difficulty level up another notch. “The sensitive nature of foldable displays means that a stylus-like input device could leave unsightly marks on the delicate screen,” he explains. Look out for #Unsightlymarksgate, coming to an excitable media outlet near you.
5. Too many novelties at once
In the Android world, the concept of the foldable is (relatively) old hat, but for Apple fans, the iPhone Ultra is going to be a lot to take in stride. Barring a few minor novelties such as the Dynamic Island, iPhones have been used in exactly the same way for almost two decades. A lot of us are going to have to update our muscle memory for an entirely new experience.
In that context, it strikes me as the height of recklessness (not to mention arrogance) to throw in an entirely new input method at the same time. Apple doesn’t need an extra usability roadbump. Not this year.

				
					

				
			This is a lot to take in.
Foundry




6. It would be an embarrassing U-turn
“If you see a stylus, they blew it.” Those were Steve Jobs’ words. And that resulted in plenty of schadenfreude when the Apple Pencil was announced a few years later.
I’ve repeatedly defended the decision to make a stylus for the iPad, which was a different use case. But making one for the iPhone really would play into the hands of the haters. Apple should stick to its guns. And its fingers.

title: Mac Studio Buyer's Guide: M5 Max vs. M5 Ultra
content:
Apple last week announced two new Mac Studio models, with one built around the M5 Max chip and one around the all-new M5 Ultra chip, replacing the M4 Max and M3 Ultra models that had been on sale since March 2025.


The gap between the two is unusually wide this time. ‌Mac Studio‌ with M5 Max starts at $2,499, holding the price Apple set when it raised Mac prices in June, while ‌Mac Studio‌ with M5 Ultra starts at $5,499, a further $200 increase on the post-June M3 Ultra price and $1,500 above what the M3 Ultra cost at launch.

memory chip shortage. Our guide helps to answer the question of how to decide which of these two ‌Mac Studio‌ models is best for you. The shared features include:


An identical enclosure measuring 3.7 inches tall and 7.7 inches wide

Neural Accelerators built into every GPU core, and hardware-accelerated ray tracing

Hardware-accelerated H.264, HEVC, ProRes, and ProRes RAW, plus AV1 decode

A next-generation SSD architecture that Apple says is up to twice as fast as before

Thunderbolt 5 with up to 120Gb/s of bandwidth, and clustering of multiple systems using RDMA (remote direct memory access)

10Gb Ethernet, HDMI, and an SDXC card slot (UHS-II)

Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 via the N1 chip, both new to the ‌Mac Studio‌

Genlock over USB-C for synchronization with professional camera capture

A 3.5mm headphone jack with support for high-impedance headphones

macOS 27, Apple Intelligence, and Siri AI



Here is everything that differs between the two models:







‌Mac Studio‌ (M5 Max)
‌Mac Studio‌ (M5 Ultra)


Starts at $2,499
Starts at $5,499


M5 Max chip
M5 Ultra chip


18-core CPU with 6 super cores and 12 performance cores
Up to 36-core CPU with 12 super cores and 24 performance cores, from 30 cores


Up to 40-core GPU, from 32 cores
Up to 80-core GPU, from 64 cores


16-core Neural Engine
32-core Neural Engine


Up to 614GB/s memory bandwidth
1.2TB/s memory bandwidth


36GB, 48GB, 64GB, or 128GB of unified memory
96GB, 256GB, or 512GB of unified memory


512GB, 1TB, 2TB, 4TB, or 8TB of storage
1TB, 2TB, 4TB, 8TB, or 16TB of storage


Up to 3.9x faster AI performance than M4 Max
Up to 4.3x the peak AI compute performance of M3 Ultra


Up to 50% faster graphics than M4 Max
Up to 1.8x faster graphics than M3 Ultra


One video decode engine and two video encode engines
Two video decode engines and four video encode engines


Two ProRes encode and decode engines
Four ProRes encode and decode engines


Four Thunderbolt 5 ports, two USB-C ports, and two USB-A ports
Six Thunderbolt 5 ports and two USB-A ports


Support for up to five 4K displays, four 6K displays, or two 8K displays
Support for up to eight 4K displays, eight 6K displays, or four 8K displays


6.0 pounds (2.7 kg)
8.0 pounds (3.6 kg)




For the overwhelming majority of buyers, including most professionals, the M5 Max is the more appropriate choice. An 18-core CPU, up to 40 GPU cores with Neural Accelerators, up to 128GB of unified memory, and up to 614GB/s of bandwidth cover workflows such as multi-stream 4K and 6K editing, large Logic sessions with real-time plugins, compiling substantial codebases, and most 3D and motion work.

Apple's own figures support this, with up to 3x faster Magic Mask performance in Blackmagic Design DaVinci Resolve Studio and 1.4x faster scene rendering in Maxon Redshift compared to M4 Max, and graphics that are up to 50% faster than the previous generation. Since memory cannot be added later, the sensible approach is to spend more on unified memory at the point of purchase rather than on the higher chip tier.

You should only choose the M5 Ultra if you anticipate running into a performance ceiling the M5 Max cannot clear. The most obvious use-case is local AI inference, where the whole model needs to be resident in memory. 256GB and 512GB configurations paired with 1.2TB/s of bandwidth allow models with hundreds of billions of parameters to run on the machine itself, which keeps sensitive material on-device and eliminates the recurring cost of paying for cloud inference.

The other workflows that can take advantage of the M5 Ultra include studios finishing 8K material from several cameras at once, where the doubled Media Engine and its four encode engines earn their keep, research and simulation work that needs an enormous memory pool, and anyone who specifically needs six Thunderbolt 5 ports or more than five displays.

There is a notable catch in how the two memory ladders overlap. The M5 Ultra begins at 96GB, which is less than the 128GB you can configure on the M5 Max, so paying the premium at the entry configuration buys you more cores and more bandwidth, but less memory. The Ultra only separates itself at 256GB and above, and Apple limits the 512GB option to the 80-core GPU model, which means the configurations that justify the machine sit far above its starting price.

This is where the price proximity argument becomes noticeable. Configuring an M5 Max with memory and storage narrows the gap considerably, and at that point the Ultra becomes worth pricing alongside it, because it roughly doubles GPU cores, Neural Engine cores, memory bandwidth, and Media Engine capacity in one step. If your workload sits comfortably inside 128GB, though, that money is better spent on storage and displays than on the chip.

Both models support clustering over Thunderbolt 5 and RDMA, and Apple says four ‌Mac Studio‌ systems working together deliver up to 3x faster AI inference than a single machine, so scaling inference does not necessarily mean buying the most expensive configuration outright.

Mac mini with the M5 Pro chip starts at $1,699 with up to a 20-core GPU and 307GB/s of memory bandwidth, which is enough for a great deal of professional work.

available to pre-order now, with availability beginning on September 22. The 512GB configuration arrives in late October, and its pricing is expected to start well above $10,000.

title: iOS 27 will actually speed up your old iPhone—here’s the proof
content:
Macworld





When Apple unveiled iOS 27 at WWDC, the main highlight was artificial intelligence, which is only available on newer phones. The company spent a good portion of its keynote talking about the new Siri AI, Apple Intelligence, and other features that require the latest hardware to run. Unsurprisingly, this left owners of older iPhones wondering what exactly they would gain from the update.
After spending some time testing the iOS 27 beta on an iPhone 11 Pro Max (the oldest iPhone supported by the update), I can report that iOS 27 is just as important for older iPhones—maybe even more so. Although they’ll miss out on the latest AI features, iOS 27 may be the best update older iPhones have received in years.
iOS 27 makes older iPhones fast again
If you’ve installed iOS 26 on an older iPhone, you’ve probably noticed that some things weren’t exactly smooth. Even some of the latest iPhones had some trouble running the fancy animations added with Liquid Glass.
Also, I recently wrote about how iOS 26 seemed noticeably buggy compared to other recent iOS releases. Animations stuttered more often, apps took longer to launch, and even basic system interactions sometimes felt sluggish.
Apple promised that iOS 27 would address many of these issues. While we only have access to the first beta of iOS 27, my tests with the iPhone 11 Pro Max show that the company was serious about improving performance, especially when it comes to old hardware.

				
					

				
			
iOS 27 will bring some design refinements to Liquid Glass, but the real improvements are with performance.

Foundry




To get a better idea of how much has changed, I measured the time it takes to complete a handful of common tasks on the same iPhone 11 Pro Max running iOS 26 and iOS 27 beta 1.
I started with something simple that most people do every day: taking photos with their iPhone. On iOS 26, my iPhone 11 took 0.98 seconds to open the Camera app, then 3.61 seconds to take a photo and load it into my photo library.
I ran the test again with iOS 27, and the improvements were noticeable. Now it only takes about 0.65 seconds to open the Camera app, and 2.44 seconds to take a photo and immediately open it from the thumbnail preview. For users, this means a lower chance of missing an important shot because their phone is too slow.
Many iPhone users also rely on the Maps app every day, and on iOS 26, the iPhone 11 took a long 3.01 seconds to load it. With the first beta of iOS 27, the same iPhone now loads the Maps app in just 1.36 seconds. That’s twice as fast as on iOS 26.
Other actions, such as launching Safari, browsing the App Store, and opening the share sheet, are also noticeably faster in iOS 27. 

iOS 27 beta vs. iOS 26 speed tests

		
			


Results are in seconds. Lower results/shorter bars are better.




On their own, these numbers won’t transform the experience. After all, we’re talking about fractions of a second in some cases. But when you’re running these tasks multiple times a day, every second adds up to minutes saved. And the whole system feels remarkably faster.
The smoother animations matter even more
Performance benchmarks are only part of the story. What really makes iOS 27 better on the iPhone 11 is how much smoother the animations feel during everyday use.
Visuals everywhere appear more consistent and less prone to frame drops. Swiping to open Control Center is noticeably more fluid. Unlocking the phone feels more responsive. App transitions seem better optimized and less likely to hitch. 
Those were all things that bothered me when I tried using this iPhone on iOS 26, and now Apple seems to have fixed nearly all of the slow animations.
Once again, these aren’t dramatic changes individually, but together they create the impression that the old hardware is no longer struggling to keep up with the operating system. The result is an iPhone that feels newer than it actually is.

				
					

				
			
You won’t get all of the features that you get on the iPhone 17 PRI Max, but iOS 27 will still be an impressive upgrade for older iPhones.

Foundry




iOS 27 also runs cooler
Another change I noticed almost immediately is the temperature. While my iPhone 11 Pro Max heats up quite easily on iOS 26, even when performing basic tasks, iOS 27 seems to keep the phone cool for longer. And that’s a great sign that the optimizations Apple made across the system have worked.
A cooler phone generally indicates that software processes are being managed more efficiently. It often means less unnecessary CPU and GPU activity, which can also translate into better battery life over time.
Of course, this is still a beta, and hardware usage can fluctuate significantly throughout the beta cycle. Still, seeing a beta run already cooler than the previous public release is an encouraging sign.
Older iPhones are getting a lot
If you watched the WWDC keynote, you might have been disappointed, as it seemed as though older iPhones wouldn’t be getting anything more than bug fixes with iOS 27. But that’s not actually the case. In fact, while devices like the iPhone 11 won’t support Siri AI, there are still many other new features coming to these devices.
One of my favorite new features in iOS 27 is the new clipboard shortcut right on the keyboard, which makes it faster to paste text or even a screenshot you just took. Being able to control the volume of the alarms and timers independently was also a nice addition.

				
					

				
			
Older iPhones won’t miss out on small iOS 27 features like this clipboard upgrade in the keyboard.

Foundry




There’s also the ability to create custom passes in the Wallet app, a redesigned interface that makes it easier to play audio messages in iMessage, an option to save a high-resolution frame from a video in the Photos app, and larger Home Screen widgets.
All of these features are coming to older iPhones with iOS 27. Sure, they might not sound as exciting as a new AI assistant that can control your phone, but they’re exactly the kind of improvements that make your phone feel more useful and polished.
Not to mention that all iPhones getting iOS 27 will feature refinements to the Liquid Glass interface, including the new transparency slider that lets you choose the look you want.
iOS 27 is a surprisingly great update for aging iPhones
To be honest, I was quite surprised when Apple confirmed during the WWDC keynote that even the iPhone 11 would get the iOS 27 update. After all, my experience running iOS 26 on that generation of phone was quite frustrating. But now that I’ve tried the first beta, I can see why Apple made that decision.
The main narrative surrounding iOS 27 focuses heavily on AI, and that’s completely understandable. Apple had been lagging behind in this race, so it’s no surprise that they want to make a big deal out of all the new Apple Intelligence and Siri AI features.

				
					

				
			
Don’t worry about missing out on Siri AI. iOS 27 is a fantastic upgrade for older iPhones.

Foundry




Yet, after using iOS 27 on an iPhone 11 Pro Max, I can’t help but think that older devices may be among the biggest beneficiaries of this update. The software feels faster. Animations are smoother. The phone runs cooler. And users still get a collection of useful new features despite missing out on AI.
For anyone worried that iOS 27 would leave older iPhones behind, the first beta suggests the opposite. Apple appears to have spent just as much time optimizing the experience for existing users as it did building features for future hardware, and that’s great news for people still holding onto a seven-year-old iPhone.

title: Apple’s loaded September kicks off with ‘huge launch’ next week
content:
Macworld





September is always the biggest month of the year for Apple fans. That’s when we get the new operating systems first announced at WWDC in June, new iPhones, new Apple Watches, and sometimes more.
This year is especially monumental. It’s the first month and the first event helmed by new CEO John Ternus, the release of the biggest OS updates in years with an all-new Siri, and the unveiling of Apple’s first folding iPhone. All that and more are coming this September. Here’s what’s on the way.
New CEO, new iPhone, and more
As of September 1, Tim Cook is out as CEO (taking a backseat role as Chairman) and new CEO John Ternus is at the helm. That means the big Apple event on September 9 will be the first not headlined by Cook in 15 years. In his welcome letter to employees, he promised a “huge launch that’s going to be phenomenal.” With Ternus at the helm, will the Surprise and Shine event be different in tone or structure from what we’ve seen the last few years? We’ll find out on September 9 at 10 am. Here’s what we expect at the event:
iPhone Ultra: The marquee product of the new lineup will be Apple’s first foldable device, likely to be called iPhone Ultra. We already have a good idea of its design, but we don’t yet know about its features, particularly what Apple is doing with the software. We expect the price to top $2,000.
iPhone 18 Pro/Max: The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will be an evolutionary upgrade from the iPhone 17 Pro. The big updates are a faster A20 Pro processor and a new main camera with variable aperture.
Apple Watch Series 12: We don’t expect much to be new about the Apple Watch Series 12. There should be a faster processor, and Apple is said to be bringing back the ceramic case option, but the rumors say not to expect a change to the design or major new features this year.
Apple Watch Ultra 4: Just like the Series 12, the new Ultra is going to be primarily a “chip and ship” update with no major design changes or new features.

				
					

				
			
Apple’s iPhone event will be loaded with shiny new products—and hopefully some surprises.

Apple




AirPods 5: Apparently, there’s an AirPods 5 that could ship as early as September. Like AirPods 4, it would come in both standard and active noise-cancelling versions, but we’re not sure what will actually be new. This is not expected to be the AirPods with cameras in them, and it’s unknown what the new features might be.
Apple TV 4K: A new-generation Apple TV box with a new processor that supports the new Siri AI is supposed to ship before the end of the year. It could be announced at the September event, or it could just go up on the website one day. There’s plenty of time for this update to be released in later months, too.
HomePod mini: Just like the new Apple TV box, the main reason for this to exist is to get a new chip that supports Siri AI. As with the Apple TV, this may not even get mentioned at the event at all and could just go up on the website as an update anytime this year.
Smart home hub: The biggest question mark for Apple’s upcoming event is whether or not the company will unveil its new home hub device. This is said to be a tablet-like pad, with a new 7-inch squarish shape, that will come in both base/speaker-mounted or wall-mounted varieties. It will run a new operating system that blends some of the features of Apple Watch and Apple TV. It’s meant to control your smart home stuff, make FaceTime calls, listen to music, and so on. Rumors say it could launch this fall, but that doesn’t necessarily mean September.
Mac mini and Mac Studio: While announced in August, the new M6 / M5 Pro Mac mini and M5 Max/Ultra Mac Studio are actually shipping starting on September 22. 
Apps and software updates

				
					

				
			
A whole new Siri is coming with iOS 27.

Apple




The OS 27 updates: All the “27” updates are getting ready for release in September. This is a huge release, with a complete overhaul for Siri, turning it into a real AI chatbot agent, as well as dozens of quality-of-life and performance improvements. There are helpful new features throughout, many of them AI-powered, like the Phone app surfacing relevant info when calling a person or business. Call the airline and get your ticket confirmation number from your email right on the Phone screen, for example. There are new Photos editing features, a totally new Image Playground, the ability to essentially vibe-code Shortcuts or Safari extensions, and over 250 other pain points and wishlist items addressed.
Siri AI: Part of the new OS 27 updates is a new Siri, appropriately called Siri AI. It’s an entirely new generation of AI assistant, and no longer years behind other contemporary AI chatbots like Gemini, Claude, or ChatGPT. It’s more conversational and has much better world knowledge, more easily understands you and your context, and can even look through your Messages, Mail, Calendar, and Contacts to piece together personalized responses. It all comes together in a new Siri app that keeps a history of your questions and chats (you can adjust for how long the history remains) and is synced between devices.
Services
Apple TV+
Here are the shows, series, and movies we expect to release on Apple TV+ in TK. If you want to know what’s coming later, check our full guide to upcoming Apple TV+ content.
Mayday: An action-packed buddy comedy film. When hotshot U.S. Navy pilot Lieutenant Troy “Assassin” Kelly (Ryan Reynolds) is sent on a top-secret mission into Russian territory at the height of the Cold War, the operation implodes, leaving him stranded behind enemy lines. September 4
Last Seen: A former police detective, now working as a dispatcher, receives a call from a teenage girl who he is convinced is his daughter, who went missing 11 years ago. September 9
Slow Horses (season 6): This darkly funny British spy thriller show is easily one of the best things on Apple TV, and it’s back for another short season. September 16
Brothers: Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrison play fictionalized versions of themselves whose lifelong friendship is thrown into chaos when they uncover a decades-old secret: They might actually be brothers. September 23
Apple Arcade
Apple releases most Apple Arcade games on the first Friday of each month. Check our Apple Arcade FAQ for a full list of Apple Arcade games and more details on the service. Occasionally, games are released with no forewarning, but you’ll usually see next month’s releases listed in the Coming Soon section.
Art of Fauna: Cozy Puzzles+: Piece together over 300 pieces of animal artwork. September 3
Block Blast+: Block-based puzzles with daily puzzles and adventure mode. September 3
Coloring Games for Families+: A very family-friendly, kid-oriented coloring game. September 3
Let’s Play! Oink Games+: 9 board games from a Japanese small-box board game company. September 3

title: Wavlink Thunderbolt 5 Dock review: Affordable, fast – now with SSD slot option
content:
Macworld





At a glance
Expert's Rating



Pros
12 ports, including four Thunderbolt 5
SSD slot option (UTD58M model)
2.5Gb Ethernet
30W USB-C at front
230W Power Delivery

Cons
Upstream port at front
Four USB-A but no USB-C
Our Verdict 
As a dual-display dock with a bunch of top-rated ports the Wavlink Thunderbolt 5 Docking Station is great value for money for 80Gbps speed and power, with a new model offering a speedy SSD slot.

What is it? A Thunderbolt 5 MacBook docking station with 12 fast ports plus an option for an SSD slot for extra affordable storage.
Who is it for? Users who require the fastest connections and those looking to add speedy storage to their MacBook setup at prices way below Apple’s own.
Who shouldn’t buy it? People who don’t need fast Thunderbolt connections or require more than two external displays.
The Wavlink Thunderbolt 5 Docking Station is a full docking station with 12 ports, including a full four 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5 and 2.5Gb Ethernet, available at an affordable price. It features a decent rack of high-end ports, and looks fancy, too.
There are two versions: the UTD58M ($349) with an integrated fast SSD slot, and the base UTD58 without ($299).
Even if your laptop has Thunderbolt 4 (TB4) rather than Thunderbolt 5 (TB5) connectivity, buying the newer faster standard will future proof your purchase. Backwards compatible with Thunderbolt 3 and 4, TB5 features the fastest 80Gbps bandwidth (up to 120Gbps Bandwidth Boost for unidirectional video) plus smart device daisy-chaining and super-fast storage connectivity.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Specs and features: The ports and power you get
One upstream Thunderbolt 5 port (80Gbps, 140W)
Two downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports (80Gbps, 15W)
One downstream Thunderbolt 5 port (80Gbps, 30W)
Four USB-A ports (10Gbps)
Ethernet (2.5Gb)
SSD slot (UTD58M model only)
UHS-II SD Card reader (312MBps)
UHS-II MicroSD Card reader (312MBps)
3.5mm audio jack
230W power supply
As well as its upstream Thunderbolt 5 port that connects to your laptop, there are three downstream TB5 ports that connect to other devices such as monitors or storage drives: one is at the front with the upstream TB5 port, and two are at the back.
Only the UTD58M model features the built-in SSD slot.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




Wavlink’s Thunderbolt 4 dock had just one downstream TB4 port as it sacrificed two possible Thunderbolt ports for dedicated HDMI 2.1 ports. With this new model, Wavlink ditches the video ports to give you the choice of which TB ports to use to connect to monitors either via a direct USB-C connection or using USB-C to DisplayPort or USB-C to HDMI adapter cables.
This gives you flexibility, and if connecting two screens we expect you’ll choose the two TB5 ports at the back.
The downstream TB5 port at the front can output at 30W, which is easily enough to fast charge an iPhone or iPad. The two TB5 ports at the back can handle 15W each.
The upstream TB5 port can output at 140W (PD 3.1), which is what you need to fast-charge the 16-inch MacBook Pro so is good for the whole range.
The external power supply can provide up to 230W of power, which is a welcome boost from the company’s rather puny 160W TB4 dock.
USB: Thunderbolt is backwards compatible with USB-C, which uses the same end connector, so any of the TB ports not being used to connect a monitor can be used for USB-C devices as well as speedy Thunderbolt. There are four speedy 10Gbps USB-A ports. USB-A has a place for legacy devices, but do we need four of them at the expense of a spare USB-C or two?

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




What are this dock’s storage options?
Both versions of the Wavlink Thunderbolt 5 Docking Station feature fast storage card readers, but only the UTD58M model comes with the built-in SSD slot hidden under its base.
This slot supports high-performance PCIe Gen 4 x4 M.2 SSD with a data transfer rate of up to 64Gbps, which should significantly improve read and write speeds with no need for a port-hogging external hard drive enclosure. Data sloggers and pro studios will enjoy the local high-speed caching.
At the time of writing you could buy a 1TB NVMe SSD for under $200, and under $400 for 2TB. 4TB SSDs will set you back more like $700, but it’s still cheaper than Apple charges at the point of purchase and gives you a lot more flexibility.
Installing your own NVMe SSD (the dock doesn’t come with one pre-installed) is simple, using the included screwdriver as shown above.
This isn’t the only Thunderbolt 5 dock with an integrated SSD slot—check out the Kensington EQ Pro Thunderbolt 5 Dock for MacBook, Ugreen Maxidok 17-in-1 dock, and Sonnet Echo 21 SuperDock—but it is the most affordable of those we have tested.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




Card readers: Although Apple’s MacBook Pro laptop includes a 250MBps card reader, having one on the dock is convenient. The Wavlink TB5 dock has two: one SD and one MicroSD, both at the fastest 312MBps. These are nicely placed at the front for easy access.
Such cards offer very affordable and extremely portable storage. At the time of writing you could get a 512GB SD card for under $50, although faster cards are pricier.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




Ethernet: While WiFi is great for phone use, sometimes hooking up to the home or office wired network gives you faster and more stable downloads. Most local area networks (LANs) use 1Gb Ethernet, known as Gigabit Ethernet or 1GbE. Increasingly networks are moving to much faster 2.5GbE, 5GbE or even 10GbE. The Wavlink Thunderbolt 5 Dock offers 2.5GbE, which is backwards compatible with 1GbE so even if you’re not yet on the faster network speed you’ll be ready for it when you do.
Other ports: At the front there’s an anti-theft Kensington Security Slot (also called a K-Slot) and a combo 3.5mm In/Out audio jack.
Wavlink dock’s display capabilities
For most people the number one reason for buying a docking station is to easily add external screens to their laptop. Connect a cable from the dock to each monitor and you massively extend your screen real estate.
While the dock can support up to three displays for Windows laptops, limitations in Apple’s setup limit you to just two, unless you install third-party software such as DisplayLink that can give you access to up to five external displays. Five!
However, for three or more monitors the dock needs to support DisplayLink, and the Wavlink Thunderbolt 5 Dock isn’t one of those. See our reviews of the best DisplayLink docks for options, but note that at the time of writing there were no Thunderbolt 5 DisplayLink docks. Your only solution for TB5 plus three displays without DisplayLink is the iVanky FusionDock Max 2, which has a nifty dual-chip arrangement that uses two of the MacBook’s Thunderbolt ports.
The Wavlink Thunderbolt 5 Dock supports up to two 6K at 60Hz displays for most M1/M2/M3 Pro/Max/ MacBooks or any M4/M5 models.
These MacBooks could opt for a single 8K/60Hz display instead.
Non-Pro/Max M1/M2/M3 MacBooks support single 4K or 6K monitors. DisplayLink is also useful if your MacBook is running one of those plain M1 or M2 processors as Apple further limits those laptops to a single display. That’s by the by as M1 MacBook owners are unlikely to be in the market for a Thunderbolt 5 dock, and it’s time we got back to the review.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




Futuristic design looks great on any desk
The Wavlink Thunderbolt 5 Dock is a smart aluminum build with some futuristic cooling vents at the top. Underneath are silicone pads that raise the dock off the desk surface for stability and further cooling. On the UTD58M the base is where you’ll find the SSD slot secured with a single screw.
I’m not a fan of having the upstream Thunderbolt port at the front of the dock as it’s the one cable you know will always be in use, so we prefer it hidden around the back. Ideally, given the choice I’d have all the Thunderbolt ports at the back and a spare USB-C port at the front for charging. But that’s not how Wavlink has laid out its ports. Still, having three downstream ports is more than some docking stations offer and we’re happy with that.
Wavlink has included an on/off button, which is appreciated. Although Apple has made the MacBook clever enough to manage its power in a sensible fashion, I still like to turn off power to the laptop’s battery as I don’t want it constantly kept filled to 100% when I’m not using it. A power button means I don’t have to yank the cable out to break the power between the dock and the laptop when I’ve finished working.
WAVLINK Thunderbolt 5 Dock (UTD58)
							

										
									Read our review
									
							
$219.99 at Amazon										 | 
										$269.99 at Newegg US										 | 
										$299.99 at Wavlink							
						
WAVLINK Thunderbolt 5 Dock with SSD Slot (UTD58M)
$349.99 at Amazon							
						
How much do the Wavlink Thunderbolt 5 docks cost?
At $299.99 or £239.99, the base-level Wavlink Thunderbolt 5 Dock is priced below most Thunderbolt 5 docks. It shares the sub-$300 price point with the Plugable Thunderbolt 5 Docking Station, and has a similar array of ports, although it has one more and faster USB-A ports. The Wavlink also wins on a higher overall power supply: 230W vs 180W.
The Plugable can stand either vertically or lie flat like the Wavlink and sensibly places the upstream TB5 port at the back. The Wavlink’s 30W front TB5 port beats the Plugable’s 15W front TB5 port. Otherwise, they are very similar in terms of tech specs.
The $349 / £349 UTD58M model with SSD slot will set you back another $50 plus the cost of whichever capacity and speed NVMe SSD that you can afford. Pay the extra $50 for the UTD58M if you want fast, inexpensive desktop storage built into the dock; otherwise the standard UTD58 offers essentially the same docking features for less.
See our roundups of the best Thunderbolt docks for Mac for other comparable solutions.
Which Wavlink Thunderbolt 5 Docking Station should you buy?
While its triple-monitor potential is muted on Macs—Apple’s limitation, not the dock’s—as a dual-display dock with a bunch of top-rated ports the Wavlink Thunderbolt 5 Docking Station and an SSD slot option is great value for money for 80Gbps speed and power. The new model with SSD slot offers high-speed data transfer and lower latency for demanding jobs with greater flexibility than you get from Apple when you purchase your Mac.

title: Should you buy a Mac mini now? M6 vs M5 Pro buying advice
content:
Macworld





The Mac mini received a major update in August 2026, so for most people this is a good time to buy. Apple announced the new M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini on August 25, 2026, with sales beginning September 22. With the next significant update unlikely for some time, there is little reason to wait for newer hardware if you need a compact desktop Mac now.
For most buyers, we recommend the M6 Mac mini. Starting at $899/£899, it is considerably more expensive than the M4 generation, which launched at $599, but it offers improved performance for everyday work, office tasks, coding, photo and video editing, and general creative use. It is particularly appealing if you already own a monitor, keyboard and mouse, or if you’re replacing an older Intel Mac or early Apple silicon model.
The M5 Pro Mac mini is better suited to more demanding users. Its additional CPU and GPU performance, Thunderbolt 5 connectivity, higher memory bandwidth and support for up to 64GB of unified memory make it a stronger choice for professional creative work, development and larger local AI models. However, with prices starting at $1,699/£1,699 and rising quickly with upgrades, most people won’t need to spend that much.
This guide explains whether to buy a Mac mini now, which M6 or M5 Pro model suits different users, what to pay, alternatives, refurbished options, drawbacks, and where to buy.


Should you buy a Mac mini now? 
There are reasons to wait. Discounts are likely to improve in the months after launch, particularly around Prime Day in October and Black Friday in November, and more refurbished or discounted M4 models may appear as buyers upgrade. If you’re happy with your current Mac, want to see independent benchmarks first or simply want the lowest possible price, there is no need to rush.
On the other hand, buyers who want a new Mac mini at launch may prefer to pre-order. A global memory shortage contributed to long delivery times and limited availability for the previous generation, and similar supply constraints could affect the new models. The higher cost of memory and other components has also contributed to the Mac mini’s substantial price increase.
Buy Mac mini now if:
You need a Mac mini now and want the latest model.
You’re replacing an Intel Mac or an older Apple silicon Mac.
You want a powerful compact desktop for everyday, office, development or creative work.
The $899/£899 M6 Mac mini provides all the performance you need.
Consider M5 Pro if:
You need more than 32GB of unified memory.
You run demanding professional creative or development workloads.
You want to run larger local AI or LLM workloads.
You need Thunderbolt 5 or substantially greater memory bandwidth.
Wait if: 
You want to see independent benchmarks of the new models.
You’re hoping for discounts around Prime Day or Black Friday.
Your current Mac still meets your needs.
You don’t need a new Mac urgently and want to see whether prices fall.
Consider refurbished if:
You can find an M4 Mac mini at a significant discount.
You want the best value rather than the newest chip.
An Apple-refurbished M4 or M4 Pro configuration meets your memory and storage needs.
You’re comfortable waiting for refurbished M6 or M5 Pro stock to appear.  


						

							




		
Apple Mac mini (M6, 2026)
$899 at Apple							
						
Apple Mac mini (M5 Pro, 2026)
$1699 at Apple							
						




						

							







Which Mac mini to buy: M6 or M5 Pro? 

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary / Foundry




The Mac mini lineup has changed significantly in 2026, with Apple introducing the M6 and M5 Pro models in August. The choice between them comes down to your workload and budget, as they serve very different audiences despite sharing the same compact design.
Apple sells two Mac mini models, both announced on August 25 and shipping from September 22, 2026:
Mac mini (M6) — starts at $899 / £899
12-core CPU, 12-core GPU
16GB unified memory (up to 32GB)
Up to 2TB SSD
Thunderbolt 4 (three ports), two front USB-C ports, HDMI, 2.5Gb Ethernet
Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6
Supports up to three displays (two 6K + one 5K)
Mac mini (M5 Pro) — starts at $1,699 / £1,699
15-core CPU, 16-core GPU (upgradeable to 18-core CPU, 20-core GPU for +$200)
24GB unified memory (up to 64GB)
Up to 8TB SSD
Thunderbolt 5 (three ports), two front USB-C ports, HDMI, 2.5Gb Ethernet
Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6
Supports up to three 6K displays
Despite the “M5” name being a generation older than “M6,” the M5 Pro is the more powerful chip — it has more CPU and GPU cores, nearly double the memory bandwidth (307GB/s vs 170GB/s), and supports far more unified memory.
Choose the M6 Mac mini if:
You don’t need more than 32GB of unified memory (RAM).
You need a compact, powerful desktop for everyday use – web browsing, office work, photo editing, coding, and general productivity.
You’re a student or budget-conscious buyer looking for the best-value option for home offices, school or office use. Education pricing brings the starting price down to $799.
You already own a monitor, keyboard, and mouse.
You don’t need the extra performance or connectivity of the M5 Pro model.
Choose the M5 Pro Mac mini if:
You’re a developer, video editor, 3D artist, musician, or researcher who needs sustained performance for demanding workloads.
You want to run larger local AI models. The M5 Pro’s higher memory ceiling and much greater memory bandwidth make it better suited to heavier LLM workloads than the M6. If local AI is a priority, choose your memory carefully because it cannot be upgraded later.
You need Thunderbolt 5 for faster external storage, high-bandwidth peripherals or professional video workflows.
You regularly work with heavy 3D rendering, high-end video production, large codebases or scientific workloads.
You need more than 32GB of unified memory.


						

							







How much should you pay for Mac mini?
M6 Mac mini, starting at $899. 
M5 Pro Mac mini, starting at $1,699. 
Since the August 2026 update, the Mac mini is no longer the budget Mac it once was. The M6 model starts at $899, $300 more than the $599 starting price of the M4 generation.
For most people, the $899 M6 Mac mini is the model to buy. It offers more than enough performance for everyday work, browsing, media and general productivity, although the standard 16GB of unified memory and 256GB SSD may feel limiting if you plan to keep it for several years.
If you need more demanding performance for creative work, development or running local AI models, the M5 Pro Mac mini starts at $1,699. Configurations with more memory and storage can quickly push the price towards $3,000, so it only makes sense if you genuinely need that extra performance.
Be cautious about spending heavily on Apple’s storage upgrades. External SSDs and Mac mini hubs with NVMe storage can provide considerably more capacity for less money.
For most buyers, we recommend spending around $899 on the M6 Mac mini. Move up to the M5 Pro only if you need its extra processing power or significantly more memory.
Discounts are likely to appear at Amazon and other resellers over time, particularly around Prime Day in October and Black Friday in November. For now, the best bargain may be a discounted M4 Mac mini, although remaining stock is likely to be limited.
Find Apple on Amazon U.S. 
Find Apple on Amazon U.K.
Students can save $100 through Apple’s Education Store, reducing the M6 Mac mini to $799 and the M5 Pro model to $1,599. Apple’s Refurbished Store is another way to save, although it may be some time before the new M6 and M5 Pro models appear there. Read: How to get an Apple student discount at Apple’s Education Store and Should you buy a refurbished Mac. 


						

							


Reasons to buy a Mac mini

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Excellent value: The price has gone up, but the Mac mini remains one of the most versatile and cost-effective ways to enter the macOS ecosystem. Even at the new starting price of $899, the Mac mini still delivers excellent performance per dollar. That balance of price, power, and efficiency is one of the main reasons for the desktop’s growing popularity. It also offers access to professional-grade performance for significantly less cash than a similarly specced MacBook Pro.
Long software support window: The M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini will have a long usable lifespan and will receive many years of macOS updates and security support. 
Compact desktop footprint: The Mac mini’s ultra-compact 5-inch square design makes it one of the most space-efficient desktop computers available. It fits easily under monitors, in small offices, or in minimalist workstation setups. Its compact form factor also makes it particularly attractive for server racks, home labs, and multi-machine deployments. 
Retail discounts and refurbished deals: Despite already offering strong value at full price, the Mac mini is occasionally discounted by third-party retailers. If you can find a Mac mini deal – even on a M4 model with a  higher-memory configuration – we recommend taking advantage of it. The Apple Refurbished Store can offer even better value, assuming stock is available. In the past, we have seen the M4 Mac mini discounted by around $100/£100, while M4 Pro models have dropped by approximately $200/£210. If deals like these reappear, they are likely worth considering.


						

							


Reasons not to buy Mac mini
The price has gone up significantly: The Mac mini was once the undisputed budget Mac, but that is much harder to say now. The entry-level model has risen sharply in price, making it less compelling for buyers primarily looking for the cheapest way into the Mac ecosystem. At $899, the latest Mac mini is still less expensive than a MacBook or iMac, but it no longer feels like the bargain it once was.
You need to buy your own peripherals: The Mac mini is a “BYODKM” – Bring Your Own Display, Keyboard and Mouse – computer. That’s central to its appeal if you already own those accessories, but it can add substantially to the cost if you don’t. Unlike an iMac or MacBook, the Mac mini doesn’t include a display, keyboard or mouse. Buying all three can easily add hundreds of dollars to the overall price. The latest models also lack USB-A ports, so you may need adapters or a hub if you still use older accessories.
It’s not portable: The Mac mini is a desktop computer, so it isn’t suitable if you need to work in different locations. You can’t easily take it to a lecture, meeting or coffee shop in the way you can a MacBook. For students, frequent travellers or anyone who regularly works away from a desk, a laptop is likely to be the better choice.
You can’t upgrade it later: You need to choose your memory and storage carefully when you buy because neither can be upgraded afterwards. Apple’s build-to-order memory and storage upgrades can also be expensive, particularly once you start moving beyond the base configuration. This can quickly push the Mac mini into MacBook Pro or Mac Studio territory. Storage is less of a concern because inexpensive external SSDs and Mac mini hubs with NVMe storage can add capacity later, but there is no equivalent workaround for unified memory.
Availability could be limited: New Mac launches can sometimes bring longer delivery times for popular configurations, particularly higher-memory or build-to-order models. The M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini may suffer significant shortages due to their popularity and the shortage of components and memory.
It’s not ideal for every AI workload: Apple is increasingly positioning its Macs for AI workloads, but as our colleagues at PCWorld explain, the Mac mini has some limitations if running large local models is your main priority. The standard M6 Mac mini tops out at 32GB of unified memory, which may be restrictive for particularly large local models. The M5 Pro model offers more memory, but higher-spec configurations become expensive quickly. There is also no support for Nvidia’s CUDA platform. Many professional AI and machine-learning tools are optimized around CUDA and Nvidia GPUs, so a Windows or Linux PC with a suitable Nvidia graphics card may be faster or better supported for some workloads. For general Apple Intelligence features and lighter local AI use, however, this shouldn’t be a concern.


						

							


What to avoid when buying a Mac mini

				
					

				
			
IDG




Intel: Avoid Intel-powered Mac mini models – when shopping for a refurbished Mac mini, prioritize models with Apple Silicon (M-series chips). 
Low RAM: We advise avoiding 8GB RAM models if possible, as newer generations now start with 16GB as the base standard. 
Check status: Additionally, ensure the device is not classified as “Vintage” or “Obsolete,” as Apple typically stops providing parts for repairs after seven to ten years. 


						

							




Is Mac mini right for you?
Is the Mac mini the best choice for you? There are a number of trade-offs to consider. 


FeatureConsideration

PortabilityNot portable; requires separate monitor, keyboard, and mouse.
ConnectivityLacks USB-A ports; may require adapters for older accessories. The M5 Pro Mac mini features three Thunderbolt 5 ports, while the standard M5model uses Thunderbolt 4. 
UpgradabilityRAM and storage are soldered and cannot be upgraded after purchase.

 



Who is the Mac mini best for?


UserRecommendation

Student, office work, web devBuy M6 Mac mini (or M4 if a refurbished model is available)
Creative work (photo/video)Buy M6 Mac mini (or M4 if a refurbished model is available)
Local AI / LLM workloadsBuy M5 Pro Mac mini 
Existing M1/M2 Mac mini ownerBuy M6 Mac mini
Intel Mac ownerBuy M6 Mac mini

 






Mac mini vs Mac Studio: Which should you buy?

				
					

				
			The Mac Studio is an even more powerful option.
Thomas Bergbold 




The choice between the Mac mini and the Mac Studio largely comes down to whether you prioritize value or maximum performance.
The Mac mini offers some of the best value in Apple’s desktop lineup. Even the standard M6 model delivers impressive performance for everyday computing, creative work, software development, and local AI tasks, while the M5 Pro configuration provides power for more demanding workloads.
The Mac Studio is designed for users who need workstation-class performance. Following the discontinuation of the Mac Pro, it is now effectively Apple’s most powerful desktop. Starting at $2,499/£2,499 for the M5 Max configuration, the Mac Studio also represents the most affordable way to get a Max-series Apple Silicon chip (which starts at $4,099/£4,099 if you buy a MacBook Pro). It is well suited to professional video production, large AI models, 3D rendering, and other heavily multi-threaded or GPU-intensive workflows.
For most users, the Mac mini is a better value purchase. However, if your workloads demand high performance, more memory and a more powerful GPU, the Mac Studio is the better choice. 


						

							


Mac mini vs MacBook Neo: Which is better value?

				
					

				
			
Thomas Armbrüster




Before the introduction of the MacBook Neo, the Mac mini was Apple’s least expensive Mac. That is no longer the case – particularly now Apple has raised the price of the entry-level Mac mini from $599/£599 to $899/£899.
The MacBook Neo is now Apple’s most affordable Mac, starting at $699/£699. It is designed as an entry-level Mac and is powered by the A18 Pro chip originally used for the iPhone 16 Pro and only offers 8GB memory. The focus is on portability, battery life, and affordability rather than performance.
The Mac mini, by contrast, remains Apple’s best-value desktop Mac for users who already own a monitor, keyboard, and mouse. Thanks to its M6 and M5 Pro chips, active cooling system, and greater performance, it is better suited to demanding workloads such as coding, creative applications, multitasking, and local AI development.


						

							


Where to buy a Mac mini 
If you’re looking to buy a Mac mini, you can choose between Apple, third-party retailers and refurbished outlets.
Apple: You can buy a Mac mini directly from the Apple Store online or at an Apple retail store. 
Apple Education Store: Apple also offers discounted education pricing for eligible students and educators via its Education Store. For example, the $899 M6 Mac mini costs $799 with education pricing.
Third-Party Resellers: It’s worth checking third-party retailers as well as Apple, as stores such as Amazon and B&H frequently discount Macs. Authorized resellers and major retailers often sell the Mac mini at less than Apple’s list price.
In the U.S., retailers include:
Amazon
Best Buy
B&H Photo Video
Costco
Adorama
DataVision
In the U.K., retailers include:
Amazon
Argos
Currys
John Lewis
AO
Ebuyer
Laptops Direct
The U.K. also has Apple Premium Resellers including KRCS, iStore, Select, Albion and Jigsaw.


						

							


Should you buy a refurbished Mac mini?
A refurbished Mac mini can be an excellent way to save money, particularly if you don’t need the latest model. Discounts can be significant, although the exact saving depends on the model, configuration and seller.
The best place to start is Apple’s Refurbished Store. Apple’s refurbished Macs are fully tested, cleaned and inspected, and come with a one-year limited warranty, 90 days of technical support and eligibility for AppleCare. They are also supplied with the appropriate accessories and repackaged in a new box.
Earlier in 2026, we saw refurbished M4 Mac mini models discounted by around $90/£90, with savings also available on the M4 Pro version. However, as of September 2026, refurbished Mac mini stock is very limited. M4 models are currently unavailable, and it may be some time before the new M6 and M5 Pro models start appearing in Apple’s refurbished store.
Availability is one of the main drawbacks of buying refurbished. Stock depends on returns and trade-ins, so you may not find the exact memory or storage configuration you want. More models may become available as owners upgrade to the latest Mac minis and older machines make their way to refurbishers.
You should also be careful when buying from third-party sellers. Refurbishment standards and warranties can vary, and marketplaces may contain much older Intel-based Mac minis. We generally wouldn’t recommend those models now unless the price is exceptionally low, as Apple silicon Mac minis offer much better performance and will receive software support for longer.
We’ve found Amazon particularly worth checking carefully. Refurbished stock can be dominated by Mac minis from 2020 or earlier, and we’ve even seen discontinued configurations listed for more than their original selling price. Always check the model year, specification and price of an equivalent new Mac before buying.
Buying refurbished is generally safer than buying second hand from a private seller. A reputable refurbished Mac should have been inspected and tested and will usually include a warranty and returns policy. A privately sold Mac may offer neither, and there is also a risk of Activation Lock if the previous owner hasn’t properly removed the Mac from their Apple Account.
Where to buy a refurbished Mac mini
U.S.: Amazon, Back Market, Best Buy, GainSaver, Mac of All Trades and Refurb.me.
U.K.: Affordable Mac, Amazon, Back Market, Hoxton Macs, MacFinder, Mac4Sale and MusicMagpie.
Read our guide to the pros and cons of buying refurbished Macs. We also have recommendations of the best places to buy a refurbished Mac.

title: Best MacBook backpacks, bags, cases and sleeves

Macworld





A good MacBook bag shares many qualities with Apple’s laptops. We want it to be tough, so it needs to be made from good materials. We want to use it for multiple tasks, so it needs to have plenty of pockets and compartments. Let’s admit it, with the diminishing number of ports on the MacBook, the bags often have the edge. And since we all admire good design here, we certainly don’t mind if the bag looks fantastic.
Plus, whatever MacBook you’ve got, Air or Pro, you’ve probably spent enough on it that you don’t want to risk it breaking—and don’t mind spending just a little more to keep it safe.
There’s no shortage of companies out there that make protective accessories for MacBooks, from laptop bags and rucksacks to sleeves, covers, and shells that clip on directly, and plenty of them do their best to be just as stylish as the Mac they’re protecting.
We’ve rounded up a selection of our favorite cases, sleeves, backpacks, roll-tops, shells and totes for the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro, whether you have a 13-, 14-, 15- or 16-inch model, to keep your Mac safe. Some might seem expensive but remember you are entrusting the bag to protect your valuable MacBook and also relieving stress on your body when carrying it. Here’s where you don’t want to skimp and risk your laptop, back and neck.
Keep reading for the full list or jump to your preferred type of laptop carrier below. A sleeve usually just protects the MacBook from scuffs and knocks when carried on its own or as further protection within a bag. Backpacks offer a lot more storage aside from your tech. Briefcases are somewhere in between and often look more business smart. We rounded up other bags such as duffles, messenger bags and totes, wheeled luggage, and finished with protective shells that encase the MacBook for all-day protection.

A roll top bag is simple to use as they have fewer straps and zips than a traditional backpack. They feature a wide top opening so you can quickly see what’s inside and make it easier to reach in and pull out your belongings. It is adjustable in volume as unused space can saved and bulking reduced by rolling up the top flap as you close it. Tighten the strap to condense the load or loosen when more space is required.
The Stubble & Co’s The Roll Top is available in either 15L, 20L or 30L capacities. We tested the spacier 20L model. That model and the 15L version are available in a wide range of smart color accents and options: Black, Yellow, Urban Green, Arctic White, Tasmin Blue, Concrete, Sand and Ember Orange. title: Apple Launching Eight New Products This Month
content:
Apple last month announced a new Mac mini and a new Mac Studio. Both machines start shipping on Tuesday, September 22, which means they will launch in the same month as new iPhones, Apple Watches, and AirPods. 


Apple is expected to introduce the unannounced products at its annual iPhone fall event, which is this year carrying the tagline "Surprise and shine." The event takes place on Wednesday, September 9, making this month one of the busiest Apple has had in a while.

We should therefore see eight new Apple products go on sale before the end of September:

Mac mini (M6 and M5 Pro): Announced last week, the new models start shipping September 22, with prices starting at $899.

Mac Studio (M5 Max and M5 Ultra): Also announced last week, the new models begin shipping September 22, with prices starting at $2,499.

iPhone 18 Pro: The flagship device set to be unveiled at Apple's fall event, with a smaller Dynamic Island and a A20 Pro chip.

iPhone 18 Pro Max: The device is rumored to gain a camera upgrade exclusive to the larger model, alongside a bigger battery.

Foldable iPhone: The company's first foldable is expected to have a ~5.5-inch display when closed, and a ~7.8-inch display when open, plus a super thin design with minimal crease and a durable hinge. It could be called "iPhone Ultra."

Apple Watch Series 12: Apple's upcoming smartwatch is expected feature fitness tracking improvements and a faster S12 chip.

Apple Watch Ultra 4: Apple's flagship rugged watch is expected to be updated alongside the Series 12, gaining the same S12 chip.

AirPods 5: The new earbuds were referenced in macOS 26.7 and are reportedly ready for release, suggesting a launch alongside the new iPhones.

Apple isn't going to release a standard iPhone 18 in September 2026. The lineup will instead focus on more expensive iPhones. The ‌iPhone 18‌, iPhone 18e, and iPhone Air 2 will come out in spring 2027 instead. Apple does not plan to refresh the Apple Watch SE this year.

Apple has held its fall event in the first two weeks of September in each of the last several years, with new iPhones going on sale the following Friday.

Bloomberg's Mark Gurman said this week he would be "very surprised" if the foldable did not come out at the same time as the Pro iPhones or "very close to it."

"Either on the same launch date, a dual launch, or coming out within weeks later. This idea of a late October, November launch, massive delays, supply chain issues, I don't believe to be the case," he said.

title: Mac App Store Apps Can Now Drop Support for Intel Macs
content:
Apple today informed developers that universal Mac App Store apps that require macOS 13 or later can remove support for Intel-based Mac computers.


We're reaching out to let you know that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now remove support for Intel-based Mac computers.


Apps that drop Intel support will no longer deliver updates for those machines, but Intel Mac users will be able to keep using the last compatible version of an app. Apple did not previously allow ‌Mac App Store‌ apps with Intel compatibility to drop support.

macOS Tahoe is the last version of macOS that will run on Intel-based Macs. macOS Golden Gate is limited to Apple silicon Macs with an M1 chip or later.

phasing out support for Rosetta 2, the feature that lets Intel-based apps run on Apple silicon Macs. Rosetta will stop working for most apps after ‌macOS Golden Gate‌, and apps that use it won't launch. Apple is making an exception for some older unmaintained gaming titles that rely on Intel-based frameworks.

title: Here's What Apple is Paying John Ternus to Run the Company
content:
Apple has set new CEO John Ternus' target compensation at $58 million, according to an updated SEC filing [PDF]. Tim Cook's target compensation is $47 million in his new role as executive chairman.


Ternus' fiscal 2027 compensation includes a $3 million salary and an annual equity award with a target value of $55 million. A quarter of the award is time-based and will vest semiannually over four years. The rest of the restricted stock units (RSUs) will vest based on Apple's total shareholder return relative to other companies in the S&P 500, which is how Cook's RSUs have worked for many years. For fiscal 2026, Apple granted Ternus a prorated RSU award with a target value of $2.5 million.

Cook's new salary will be $2 million, but he's also earning an equity award with a target value of $45 million in fiscal 2027. Half will be granted in the form of time-based RSUs that vest over four years, and the other half will vest based on Apple's stock performance. Should Cook retire on or after the first anniversary of the grant date, his equity will vest, but he won't receive the shares until the originally scheduled vesting dates. 

Target compensation figures for Ternus and Cook do not include performance-based bonuses, so the final amount each earns in fiscal 2027 could change.

title: John Ternus is the perfect CEO for this Apple era
content:
Macworld





After 15 years at the helm, Tim Cook stepped down as Apple CEO today. In his stead is John Ternus, an Apple veteran who most recently served as Apple’s head hardware honcho and has been knocking around the hallways in Cupertino for most of his adult life. If there’s anyone who knows Apple as well as Cook, it’s Ternus.
What can we expect going forward? Tim Cook was effusive in his praise of Ternus, writing in his final message to employees as CEO, “I will miss leading you and being with you for every step, even as I take enormous comfort in handing the helm to someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John. Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does and I could not be more excited for his leadership.”
But what will the John Ternus era really look like? Will he be able to correct Apple’s mistakes and put the company on the path to further prosperity? And what will that future look like for you? I’ve gazed into the tea leaves, examined my fair share of entrails and read every palm I can find to see if I can work it all out. Here’s what I reckon we could be in for.
Who is John Ternus?
Until being named as CEO, John Ternus was Apple’s Senior Vice President of Hardware Engineering, and he’s overseen the physical products that have made Apple such a success. (Apple announced that Johny Srouji will succeed Ternus as hardware chief.)
He first joined Apple in 2001 as part of the company’s product design team, with a particular focus on the much-loved Cinema Display. He graduated to Vice President of Hardware Engineering in 2013 and was then promoted to Senior Vice President of Hardware Engineering in 2021.
As the hardware engineering lead, he at first handled Apple’s AirPods, iPad and Mac hardware divisions. iPhone hardware was added to that roster in 2020, with the Apple Watch being put under his purview in 2022. He also played a leading role in Apple’s transition away from Intel processors and towards Apple silicon, taking to the stage and conducting interviews to promote the new chips.
And since the ouster of John Giannandrea as Apple’s AI chief in 2025, the company’s secret robotics projects have been moved under Ternus’s aegis, too.

				
					

				
			
John Ternus played an instrumental role in the Apple silicon transition for the Mac.

Apple




At 51, he’s also one of the youngest members of Apple’s senior leadership team and taking ober at almost the exact same age as Tim Cook was when he became CEO in 2011, 15 years ago. That tells you that in making this move, Apple is planning for the long haul. If all goes well for the company, Ternus could be in charge for the next decade and a half, if not more.
The John Ternus era
Tim Cook is many things, but unlike Steve Jobs, he’s never truly been a product person. Ternus is a hardware guy through and through, however, and this could help him fix some of Apple’s most pressing problems, such as its floundering Vision Pro and how it makes its forthcoming augmented reality glasses a rip-roaring success.
On that topic, it’s worth noting that the first role Ternus took on after graduating from university was at Virtual Research Systems, a company focused on making virtual reality headsets and other devices. Could that give him uncommon insight into how Apple can set the beleaguered Vision Pro on the right path?
Maybe, maybe not. Ternus left Virtual Research Systems to join Apple in 2001, and a huge amount has changed in the VR world since then. At the same time, Ternus was at Apple during the entire Vision Pro creation process and would have had a strong role in its development. If he were present in a leadership position during that time, would much change now that he’s set to head up the company?
I wouldn’t rule it out. His nature as a product person could give him the ideas and vision to correct course now that he’s got more power concentrated in his hands. It could also be exactly what’s needed to steer the long-rumored Apple smartglasses to a successful launch.
And there’s an encouraging tidbit from a New York Times profile of Ternus from earlier this year. There, it was noted that around 2018, Apple was thinking of adding a LiDAR Scanner to its iPhones but was concerned that the relatively expensive $40 component would eat into its profits. Ternus proposed that the part could be limited to the Pro models and excluded from the entry-level iPhones.
But crucially, he didn’t do this purely because he was looking out for Apple’s bottom line. According to the Times’ profile, Ternus’s reasoning was that the Pro-level iPhones “tended to be purchased by Apple’s most loyal customers, who would be excited about new technology. Average consumers, on the other hand, probably wouldn’t care.”
That’s telling because it reveals Ternus’s sure-footed understanding of Apple’s customers and what they do and do not care about.

				
					

				
			
John Ternus seems to have an understanding of Apple customers and what they want in their products.
Apple
Apple is often accused of being so obsessed with being the best that it becomes too premium, making its devices unaffordable for most people. But if Ternus can take the insight demonstrated in the Times’ profile and apply it to the rest of Apple’s products going forward, we can perhaps hope for a company that remains strongly in touch with what its base wants.
Ternus has also come out swinging in the right to repair debate, saying that Apple’s aim is to improve product durability rather than increase repairability, which can add points of failure and “unintended consequences that are worse for the consumer and worse for the planet.” That doesn’t mean repairability concerns will be thrown by the wayside — the MacBook Neo, after all, is one of the most repairable Apple devices in years. Yet with Ternus’s focus on device quality and longevity, the emphasis will likely be placed elsewhere.
More than just hardware
Ternus’s tenure as hardware chief hasn’t been perfect, of course. He pushed hard for infamous missteps like the MacBook Pro’s Touch Bar and butterfly keyboard, both of which are now viewed as major missteps.
There are unanswered questions, like whether he holds the same deep commitment to privacy, accessibility and environmental action as Tim Cook. It would be no surprise if he does, as it would be highly unusual for Cook to choose a successor who is not on board with these issues. But it’s still something of an unknown for now.

				
					

				
			
Can John Ternus lead Apple into areas where the company has fallen short?

Apple




And for all of Ternus’s hardware expertise, many of Apple’s biggest problems lie in software, with AI and its Liquid Glass design being particularly front-of-mind. Yet even here, there are promising signs. Apple is a highly integrated company that controls both its hardware and software. You might be a “hardware person” like Ternus, but you’re not shut off in a quarantine, never to touch software.
We can see that in Ternus’s own history. According to Bloomberg, Ternus was one of the strongest voices within Apple who pushed for the creation of iPadOS. Ternus argued that the iPad wouldn’t be able to live up to its potential and take advantage of its hardware capabilities if it did not have its own bespoke operating system. In other words, Ternus understood how hardware and software can help each other thrive. That’s the ideal mindset to have at a company like Apple.
As well as that, one of Ternus’s extra roles is as “executive sponsor” for design. While that doesn’t mean he’s a designated design guru along the lines of Jony Ive or Alan Dye, it does mean that he’s tasked with handling design issues (both hardware and software) during executive meetings. So, while his focus has remained on hardware, he’s been dipping his toes into software issues for some time now.
Interestingly, Apple’s most recent CEOs have all specialized in slightly different disciplines. For Jobs, it was design and marketing. For Cook, operations. And in Ternus’s case, it’s hardware. I know that’s something of a simplification, but it’ll be intriguing to see how Ternus’s background will impact the way he approaches his new job.
With Tim Cook’s tenure coming to an end and John Ternus stepping further into the limelight, we could be on the cusp of major change at Apple. But given all we know about the company’s new CEO, from his passions and priorities to the way he is focused on hardware without excluding everything else, Apple looks to be in safe hands.

title: Read John Ternus' First Memo to Apple Employees as CEO
content:
John Ternus officially became Apple's CEO today, with Tim Cook transitioning to a new role as Executive Chair. Ternus sent his first memo as CEO to employees this morning, praising Cook and sharing his excitement for Apple's future.


MacRumors obtained a copy of the memo, which you can read in full below.
Team,

Today, on my first day as CEO, I just wanted to send a quick note to thank everyone for the warm wishes. I also want to extend my deep appreciation to Tim for sharing so much of his knowledge and experience during this transition, and more importantly, for everything he contributed to Apple over the years. We're so lucky to have had a CEO who led with his values and with such decency and humanity. We are all better for it, and I'm so grateful he'll be our executive chairman.

I'm honored to be stepping into this role at what is truly the greatest company in the world, and I am so excited about everything we have in store. We have a huge launch next week that's going to be phenomenal. Thanks for everything you've all done to make it possible.

I'm just as excited about what lies beyond that, including the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven't even imagined yet that we'll dream up and create together. There's no team in the world I'd rather build the future with.

More to come. In the meantime, thanks for your excellent work!

Ternus is a longtime Apple employee, having first joined the company in 2001. Prior to becoming CEO, he was senior vice president of Hardware Engineering, so he has a product-focused background instead of the operations background Cook has. Apple's leadership team has been reorganizing during the transition from Cook to Ternus, and the full effect of the changes will play out over the next several years.

Hardware Engineering team that Ternus previously led. Former engineering VP and Ternus lieutenant Laura Legros is returning to Apple, and the product design team was restructured.

Cook told employees he took "enormous comfort" in handing leadership of Apple to "someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John."

Bloomberg says Cook liked to keep departing executives in smaller roles, but Ternus may not continue that practice.

title: It might be trivial to make custom-fit AirPods in the future
content:
Apple has been continuing to research AirPod design in the hunt for the best fit for most users, but now it may have a way to personalize the earbuds for every individual wearer. The question is how to get precise ear measurements for millions of users.


Detail from the patent showing that fabric AirPods would still retain the basic shape of the current models - image credit: Apple.
As AirPods and AirPods Pro have continued to improve their sound quality, Apple has also attempted to make them fit better in users' ears. Now a newly-granted patent called "Fabric-based earbuds" proposes the novel solution of customizing every pair for every buyer.
"An electronic device with a three-dimensional sensor may be used to capture three-dimensional images of one or both of the user's ears," says the patent. "The three-dimensional ear images may be provided to computing equipment that analyzes the images to determine the dimensions of the ear such as tragus and antitragus dimensions and concha dimensions."

content:

Ternus joined Apple in 2001, became a vice president of hardware engineering in 2013, and became senior vice president of hardware engineering in 2021. He is 51, so he could serve as CEO for 10 to 15 years before reaching typical retirement age.
